passages.t: Even Moses and Samuel could not turn it
passages.happening:
The LORD tells Jeremiah that even if Moses and Samuel stood before him, his heart would not go out to this people (verse 1). If they ask where they should go, they will hear: those destined for death, to death; for the sword, to the sword; for famine, to famine; for captivity, to captivity (verse 2). God will make them a horror to the kingdoms of the earth ‘because of what Manasseh son of Hezekiah king of Judah did in Jerusalem’ (verse 4).

‘Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem? Who will mourn for you?’ (verse 5). They have turned their backs, and God is weary of relenting (verse 6). He will scatter them with a winnowing fork at the gates of the land (verse 7). Widows will be more numerous than the sand of the sea (verse 8). The mother of seven will grow faint, ‘Her sun will set while it is still day’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Moses and Samuel were remembered as Israel's great intercessors. Moses stood between the people and God's anger after the golden calf, and Samuel prayed for Israel and promised never to stop. To say that even they could not change God's mind was the strongest possible way to say the verdict was settled.

Manasseh reigned for about fifty-five years in the first half of the seventh century BC, the longest reign of any king of Judah, while Judah was subject to Assyria. Kings charges him with rebuilding the shrines Hezekiah had torn down, sacrificing his own son and filling Jerusalem with innocent blood. Verse 4 traces the coming disaster to the long road his reign began.

The winnowing fork tossed grain in the wind so the chaff blew away. A mother of seven was the picture of a full and happy family in the ancient world; her sun setting at noon is the end of everything she had.
passages.later: Samuel had said, ‘far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you’ (1 Samuel 12:23). Kings records that Manasseh ‘shed so much innocent blood that he filled Jerusalem from end to end’ (2 Kings 21:16).
passages.asks: Even the greatest intercessors could not turn this judgment aside. Ask what it means that some consequences cannot be prayed away. And ask whose long-ago choices are still shaping the place you live, and what you are passing on.

passages.t: God's words a joy, and God like a mirage
passages.happening:
Jeremiah cries out. ‘Woe to me, my mother, that you have borne me, a man of strife and conflict in all the land’ (verse 10). He has neither lent nor borrowed, yet everyone curses him.

The LORD says he will deliver him for good and make his enemies plead with him in their distress (verse 11). Can anyone smash iron from the north (verse 12)? Judah's treasures will be given up as plunder, and the people enslaved in a land they do not know (verses 13 and 14).

Jeremiah prays. ‘You understand, O LORD; remember me and attend to me. Avenge me against my persecutors’ (verse 15). ‘Your words were found, and I ate them. Your words became my joy and my heart’s delight’ (verse 16). He never sat with the revelers; because God's hand was on him, he sat alone (verse 17). ‘Why is my pain unending, and my wound incurable, refusing to be healed? You have indeed become like a mirage to me’ (verse 18).

God answers. ‘If you return, I will restore you; you will stand in My presence’ (verse 19). If he speaks what is noble and not worthless, he will be God's spokesman (verse 19). God will make him a fortified wall of bronze; they will fight him but not overcome him, for God is with him to save and deliver him (verses 20 and 21).
passages.hearers:
This is the second of Jeremiah's confessions. Lending and borrowing were the usual causes of quarrels between neighbors; Jeremiah has done neither, and still everyone curses him.

To eat God's words meant to take them in completely. The same picture appears when Ezekiel eats a scroll. The words were Jeremiah's joy, and they also cut him off. He sat alone while others celebrated.

A mirage, or a brook that fails, was a cruel thing in that land: a stream bed that ran in winter and was dry in summer, so a traveler counting on it found nothing. Jeremiah says God has been like that to him.

God's answer uses the word return, the word Jeremiah has been preaching to the people. Now the prophet himself must return. The promise of verse 20 repeats the words of his call in chapter 1.
passages.later: Ezekiel ate the scroll God gave him, ‘and it was as sweet as honey in my mouth’ (Ezekiel 3:3). A psalm of the dark also asks God, ‘Why do You hide Your face from me?’ (Psalm 88:14).
passages.hard:
Is it wrong for Jeremiah to call God a mirage, and why does God tell him to return?

Jeremiah's complaint is shocking, and the Bible keeps it. Faithful people in Scripture speak to God with this honesty (Psalm 88, Job, Habakkuk), and God does not treat lament as rebellion. Yet God's reply in verse 19 does call Jeremiah to turn back and to speak what is precious rather than worthless. Interpreters differ on what needed correcting. Some think it was the charge that God cannot be trusted; others think it was the self-pity and the wish for revenge in verse 15; others see a prophet close to giving up his calling.

God's rebuke comes with restoration, not rejection: if Jeremiah returns, God will restore him and be with him. The chapter holds together the freedom to bring any complaint to God and the need to let God answer it.

If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jeremiah found joy in God's words and still felt God had failed him. Ask whether you have felt both of those at once. And ask what it would mean for you to return and let God restore you, rather than leave your calling.
